intro: You are Stephen, a physicist in Cambridge whose work takes place in your head and on a blackboard, and whose way to the lecture hall is full of stairs. People around you make a lot of your work possible, and some do not wait to hear you finish a sentence.

ladder.why: A wheelchair user cannot climb a tree-house ladder. The way up was built for others.

market.why: Noisy crowds talk over a man who speaks through a synthesiser. Getting heard takes extra time.

quiet.why: Long, calm hours of thinking and equations were where Stephen worked best.

bridge.why: Colleagues, students, nurses and family carried the work forward, like a bridge.

advantage.title: Right question
advantage.text: Stephen's strength was asking the right question and narrowing a huge problem down. Remove one wrong answer before you choose.

life.title: Oxford, 1942
life.text: Stephen is born on 8 January 1942 in Oxford to two scientists. At school in St Albans he loves board games and taking things apart, and classmates jokingly call him "Einstein".

life.title: Cambridge, 1962
life.text: Stephen starts a PhD in cosmology. In 1963, aged 21, he is diagnosed with motor neurone disease, and doctors expect him to live about two more years. He keeps studying and working.

life.title: Old buildings, no ramps
life.text: As he starts using sticks and then a wheelchair, Cambridge's old buildings turn into obstacles: steps, narrow doors, no lifts. Everyday tasks need planning and help from others.

life.title: People around him
life.text: He gets engaged to Jane Wilde and they marry in 1965. Friends, family and fellow students help with daily life, which leaves more of his energy for physics.

life.title: Black holes leak
life.text: In 1974 Stephen shows that black holes are not completely black. At 32 he becomes one of the youngest Fellows of the Royal Society.

q.q: What did Stephen show about black holes in 1974?
a: They slowly give off energy, now called Hawking radiation
They are the same as white dwarf stars
q.x: Hawking radiation means black holes slowly lose energy and can eventually evaporate. It was a surprise to many physicists.

life.title: Newton's old chair
life.text: In 1979 Stephen takes up a famous professorship at Cambridge and keeps it for 30 years.

q.q: Which professorship, once held by Isaac Newton, did Stephen hold?
q.x: The Lucasian chair of mathematics was created in 1663. Newton held it before Stephen did.

life.title: Geneva, 1985
life.text: Severe pneumonia during a trip to Switzerland leads to a tracheotomy, and Stephen can no longer speak. He needs round-the-clock nursing and a new way to communicate, and nobody has built one for him yet.

life.title: A voice from a computer
life.text: A program called Equalizer lets him choose words with a hand clicker, later with a sensor on his cheek. A speech synthesiser speaks them. He keeps its American-accented voice because it feels like his own.

life.title: Spoken over
life.text: Many people who use speech devices report that strangers talk to their carer instead of to them, or assume they understand less. Patience would cost nothing. (A common experience, not a documented event.)

life.title: A Brief History of Time
life.text: His 1988 book explains the universe to everyone and sells over 25 million copies. A scientist who cannot speak aloud becomes one of the best-known voices on Earth.

life.title: Paralympics, 2012
life.text: Stephen speaks at the opening of the London Paralympics. He urges people to look up at the stars and not down at their feet, and to be curious. He also speaks for access to healthcare and technology for disabled people.

life.title: 2018: Westminster Abbey
life.text: Stephen Hawking dies on 14 March 2018, aged 76, 55 years after the doctors' first forecast. His ashes are placed in Westminster Abbey near Newton and Darwin. His work belongs to a whole team of people.

sources: Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time (1988) and My Brief History (2013)
flags: Paralympics 2012 speech wording is paraphrased; docs/characters.md says to verify the exact quote.
Station 'Spoken over' is a general experience, not a dated event; marked as such in the text.
